item.title: Cowboys countdown to kickoff: Top 100 iconic games – Day 6
item.description: We countdown 100 days until kickoff with a series of the most iconic games in Cowboys history. Today is Day 6
item.content:encoded:
It is Day 6 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like how big the game was for the organization, how memorable the game was, games that had unusual events take place, games that are a part of NFL lore, Cowboys firsts, and games where the Cowboys just plain dominated. Variety is the spice of life and we have all different kind of Cowboys games to review. At the bottom, we’ll link each day of the countdown so you can go back and check out any you missed.

Things really heat up now as we reach Day 6 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff, when we revisit a play so significant that its nickname became permanent football language. With Dallas trailing Minnesota and its season only seconds from ending, Roger Staubach launched a desperate pass toward Drew Pearson. The “Hail Mary” was officially born. 

Sunday, December 28, 1975 — 2:00 p.m. ET

Metropolitan Stadium, Bloomington, Minnesota

Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 17, Minnesota Vikings 14

Dallas, a 10-4 wild-card team, faced one of the league’s strongest opponents, Minnesota. Minnesota had gone 12-2, boasting the NFC’s best record and featuring league MVP Fran Tarkenton. Their defense, which allowed the fewest yards in football, made life extremely difficult for Staubach and the Cowboys throughout the afternoon.

The first half was dominated by defense. Minnesota eventually received a huge break when a punt bounced near Cliff Harris. Dallas lineman Pat Donovan attempted to recover it, but the loose ball escaped him, allowing Minnesota to recover at the Cowboys’ four-yard line. Chuck Foreman scored from one yard out shortly after, giving the Vikings a 7-0 lead that held through halftime. 

Dallas finally produced a sustained drive after the break. A late-hit penalty following a Preston Pearson reception helped move the Cowboys downfield before Doug Dennison scored on a four-yard run to tie the game. Toni Fritsch then kicked a 24-yard field goal early in the fourth quarter, putting Dallas ahead 10-7.

Minnesota responded with its best offensive possession of the game. Tarkenton directed an 11-play, 70-yard drive before Brent McClanahan powered across from one yard with 5:24 remaining. The Vikings had regained a 14-10 lead, and after Dallas went three-and-out on its next possession, Minnesota appeared capable of simply running out the clock. 

With the Cowboys defense providing a final chance, Minnesota faced third-and-two before the two-minute warning. They attempted to keep the ball in Tarkenton’s hands, but Charlie Waters broke through Foreman’s block and dropped the quarterback for a three-yard loss. This forced the Vikings to punt, and Dallas took possession at their own 15 with 1:51 remaining and no timeouts. 

The final drive nearly ended before the famous play ever happened. After moving the ball to the Dallas 31, Staubach mishandled a low shotgun snap and lost eight yards. The Cowboys eventually faced fourth-and-16, when Staubach found Pearson near the sideline for 25 yards.

After an incompletion, Dallas had time for one desperate shot. Staubach dropped back, pump-faked and launched deep down the right sideline toward Pearson. The pass came down around the Minnesota five as Pearson and Wright made contact. Wright fell, Pearson secured the underthrown football against his body and ran untouched into the end zone for a 50-yard touchdown with 24 seconds remaining. No offensive pass interference was called, despite furious protests from the Vikings. 

Afterward, Staubach explained that he had closed his eyes and said a “Hail Mary” after releasing the football. Staubach’s description of the play helped transform Hail Mary into the universally understood football term for a last-chance desperation pass.

This game belongs near the very top of the countdown because its influence extends beyond Cowboys history. Dallas did not simply win an extraordinary playoff game, Staubach and Pearson created a moment whose name became shorthand throughout the sport. Every time a quarterback launches one final desperation pass toward the end zone, the connection between number 12 and number 88 lives on.

Interesting Facts About the Game

Pearson entered Dallas’ final possession without a reception and then caught four passes for 91 yards on the winning drive.

item.title: New York Jets: Questions, Questions Everywhere
item.description: The Jets have questions. Do they have the right answers?
item.content:encoded:
A new season is about to get underway for the New York Jets, and with it come questions. Every season brings new questions, but this season just feels different in the magnitude of uncertainty surrounding the team. Some years, like in the 2010 season, the Jets had established veterans at most key positions. The talent was in place, the coaching was sound, at least on the defense, and we knew going in this was a team that, barring catastrophic injuries, was built to compete at the highest levels. Other seasons, like many of the last 15 years, the talent level was very low, the coaching was abysmal, and we knew going in that the team had very little chance to succeed.

This year feels different. There seem to be questions at almost every level of the organization. Uncertainty seems extremely high. If most of the major questions are resolved to the upside, this could be an interesting and competitive team. If most of the major questions are resolved to the downside, this could be another season where the Jets are vying for one of the top spots in the upcoming NFL draft. Let’s take a look at some of the most pressing questions facing the Jets.

Coaching

It all starts at the top. Head coach Aaron Glenn had a concerning year in 2025, his first as an NFL head coach. Coming into the season cocky and adversarial with all who dared question him, Glenn was soon humbled by a team that ended up in the conversation for worst team in the NFL. When the trade deadline approached it was clear the team was really, really bad, and the Jets threw in the towel on the 2025 season by trading their two best players on defense, Quinnen Williams and Sauce Gardner. At that point, the defense utterly collapsed, putting forth one noncompetitive performance after another. A large part of this was clearly a lack of talent, but the coaching can’t completely escape blame. Once the season was over Glenn massively overhauled the coaching staff, bringing in new coaches at every level, including replacing the offensive and defensive coordinators.It is a bit odd for a head coach to need to fire nearly every coach he handpicked himself just a year earlier.

Now Glenn may be on the hotseat. He likely will not survive another disastrous season. Can Glenn learn from his many mistakes of 2025? Will his new coaching staff prove to be more competent than last year’s crew? Is defensive playcalling really a Glenn superpower? Will the Jets look better prepared? Will they at times look like they have outcoached the opposition? Will they be better tacklers? Will the young players successfully develop?

The head coach is a big part of any team’s success. Glenn did not look the part of a top head coach last season. Heck, he didn’t look the part of a competent head coach last season. How he learns from his mistakes and grows as a head coach will go a long way to determining the level of success or failure the Jets achieve this year.

OFFENSE

Quarterback

Last season the Jets had an atrocious Justin Fields, a washed up Tyrod Taylor, and a practice squad level Brady Cook share the quarterback position. It did not go well.

All three of those guys are now gone. In their place the Jets have acquired veteran Geno Smith via trade and rookie Cade Klubnik in the draft. Klubnik is probably not ready to play extensive snaps this season. That puts it all on Geno Smith.

Geno Smith enjoyed a modicum of success with the Seattle Seahawks from 2022 through 2024 before the Seahawks decided to move on after the 2024 season. Former Seahawks head coach latched on with the Las Vegas Raiders, and he brought Geno Smith with him as the new Raiders starting quarterback. It did not go well.

In 2025 Geno Smith started 15 games for the Raiders and led them to a 2-13 record in those games. He led the NFL in sacks and interceptions, an unfortunate duo of leading stats for Smith. Smith posted just 3025 passing yards and a career low 34 QBR. It was a bad performance for Smith, but there were pretty significant mitigating factors.

Smith played behind arguably the worst offensive line in the NFL. His leading receivers were Brock Bowers, who was hobbled by injuries much of the season, Jakobi Meyers, who was traded after just seven games, and Tre Tucker. This was a terrible offensive environment. Any quarterback would have struggled. One season prior Smith led the Seahawks to a 10 – 7 record while passing for more than 4300 yards. The question now becomes, what can Smith produce for the Jets?

Certainly the Jets will provide Smith a significantly better offensive line. Barring significant injuries the Jets should also provide Smith with better weapons. Unless the Jets suffer a rash of major injuries Smith should be better in 2026, but how much better? Smith will turn 36 years old this October. Age related decline is likely already taking place. Smith’s QBR has declined in each of the last three years. At this point Smith’s ceiling is likely something like a league average starting quarterback, which would be a major improvement on the dreck the Jets have been trotting out there in recent years. The question is, what is the floor? The answer will go a long way to determining the Jets’ fate in 2026.

Offensive Line

The offensive line has relatively few questions, a refreshing change from the recent past. Center Josh Myers is subpar, and new guard Dylan Parham is coming off a down year after a pretty good 2024. Will Parham rebound?

Guard Joe Tippman is better than average and still improving. The two tackles, Armand Membou and Olu Fashanu, are young, ascending and talented. The depth isn’t great, but that is a league wide problem at offensive line. Bottom line, this is likely to be at least a league average unit with potential to develop into much better than average. Provided they avoid too many injuries, if the Jets offense fails, it is unlikely the offensive line will be a significant culprit.

Running Backs

Like the offensive line, this is a young and solid unit. Starter Breece Hall is a borderline top ten back. The perennially overlooked Isaiah Davis has quietly produced excellent play as Hall’s backup. He may be capable of more. Braelon Allen is the primary question here. Touted as a talented power back when he was drafted two years ago, Allen has failed to impress in his two years in the NFL. Now in his third year and coming into camp bigger and stronger than ever, this feels like a make or break season for Allen. Can he live up to prior expectations and develop into one of the better power backs in the NFL? If he does the Jets might have a running game that goes a long way towards taking the pressure off Geno Smith.

Wide Receivers

As usual, this group boils down to Garrett Wilson and a whole lot of questions. What seems different this year is the upside appears significantly greater. 

Adonai Mitchell has been unable to put it all together since he was drafted two years ago. He was buried on the Indianapolis Colts depth chart to start his career, then came over to the Jets in the Sauce Gardner trade last year. With Garrett Wilson sidelined by injury, Adonail Mitchell became the de facto WR1 for the Jets the rest of the season, and he did not thrive in that role. In eight games with the Jets Mitchell produced just two games with more than three receptions and just two games with more than 43 receiving yards. He caught just 41% of his targets, produced an abysmal 5.2 yards per target, and his quarterbacks had an unholy 41 passer rating throwing to Mitchell.

Those are frighteningly bad numbers for a wide receiver, but there was one huge mitigating factor. The starting quarterbacks for Mitchell were the aforementioned Justin Fields (one game), Tyrod Taylor (three games) and Brady Cook (four games). There is no doubt those quarterbacks hurt the performances of every receiver on the Jets. The question is, what can Mitchell be with a competent starter? Rumors out of 2026 training camp are optimistic about Mitchell for 2026, but until we actually see it when the games count, Mitchell remains something of a mystery who struggles with contested catches, drops and physical coverage.

Rookie Omar Cooper is penciled in as the likely WR3 for this team, but he had a quiet training camp and there are questions as to how NFL ready he will be out of the gate. Isaiah Williams is a nice story who has worked his way up the depth chart and is challenging Omar Cooper for the WR3 spot. Can he be a difference maker in the NFL? Probably not, but we have yet to see the extent of his upside. 

Arian Smith and Tim Patrick aren’t so much question marks as afterthoughts. If the Jets need to rely on either of these two for significant roles in the passing game that will spell trouble.

Tight Ends

The Jets tight ends are nothing but question marks. Rookie Kenyon Sadiq was selected by the Jets with the 16th overall pick in the 2026 NFL draft. That kind of draft capital spent on a tight end is rare and usually presages great expectations. Unfortunately Sadiq missed virtually the entire offseason and is now playing catch up. We are unlikely to see Sadiq in a major role early on in the season given how behind he is with the offense. The question is, how quickly can Sadiq catch up and can he deliver the kind of game changing results the Jets think he’s capable of this season, or will we have to wait another year to see Sadiq’s upside?

Second year tight end Mason Taylor will continue as the Jets TE1, at least until Sadiq is ready. Taylor had a serviceable but uninspiring year in 2025, struggling with drops and failing to produce many big plays. The question is, how much more can he be? The Jets drafted Taylor to be a difference maker. Tight ends often struggle as rookies, but by the second year you often start to see the upside. Can Taylor produce a second year leap?

DEFENSE

Safeties

The 2025 Jets had a horrendous collection of safeties. The Jets tried to address that by bringing in Minkah Fitzpatrick and Dane Belton. Fitzpatrick is obviously a top talent. The question is, at age 29 is he in decline? Fitzpatrick spent a lot more time close to the line of scrimmage last year, and his performance rebounded over a down year the year prior. Is Fitzpatrick mostly a guy the Jets play close to the line of scrimmage now? If so, who can play the deep safety role? Andre Cisco was brought in last season to fill that role, but he has been just plain bad as a deep safety his entire career. Cisco sports an unsightly 120 passer rating when targeted for his career (Yikes!). Relying on him to be the last line of defense is ill advised. Newly acquired Dane Belton had a great camp, but he is a guy you want near the line of scrimmage. Playing Belton deep seems like an option fated for misadventure. The final option is second year safety Malachi Moore, who seemingly has fallen out of favor with the Jets. Bottom line here: there are big questions as to who will provide the last line of defense for the Jets. Fitzpatrick seemingly does not want the role and may be aging out of it, and every other option seems to invite disaster. 

Cornerbacks

This is another position with nothing but questions. The starters appear to be Brandon Stephenson, Azareye’h Thomas and Jarvis Brownlee. Stephenson is the only established starting cornerback in that group. However, he is established in less than an ideal way. Stephens has established that he is not a starting caliber cornerback. Last season Stephens allowed a 134 passer rating when targeted (double yikes!). Can he develop into a better cornerback? Not likely. Stephens will turn 29 years old in December. At that age he is more likely to already be in decline than to be ascendant.

Brownlee was surprisingly effective in seven games in the slot with the Jets last season, allowing just 5.4 yards per target and an 84 passer rating. If he could perform like that in the long run that would be outstanding, but Brownlee has just 18 NFL starts under his belt and his prior work with the Titans was not nearly as promising. It’s difficult to know what to expect out of Brownlee.

The same goes for Thomas, who was quite good in just five starts as a rookie last season, allowing just an 84 passer rating and 48% completion percentage. It’s a very small sample, and Thomas has a pretty major known weakness in his pedestrian speed. With less than ideal deep safety options backing him up, that lack of speed could become Thomas’ downfall, but if he can hold up as well as he did in his few starts last year, the Jets may have something.

The primary backups at cornerback, Nahshon Wright and DeAngelo Ponds, provide more questions than answers. Ponds is very small for an NFL cornerback. In addition, like Sadiq, he has missed nearly the entire offseason and is playing catch up. Ponds is unlikely to play a major role early on. Who knows when or if he will take on a starting role this season? If he does, who knows if he can hold up in coverage against NFL receivers? 

Wright led the NFL in interceptions last season with five, but when he wasn’t intercepting passes he was getting burned a lot. Wright, who turns 28 years old in September, earned a starting role for the first time in his career last year with the Bears. He certainly was a playmaker for the Bears, but he also was problematic in coverage. Wright gave up 813 yards in coverage and allowed a very poor 8.3 yards per target. Other than interceptions Wright offers very little as a cornerback. Can he continue to force turnovers for the Jets?

Linebackers

The Jets brought in Demario Davis in free agency after Jamien Sherwood failed in 2025. Davis no doubt brings durability, sure tackling and effective overall play at linebacker. However, Davis will turn 38 years old in January and is pretty clearly in decline. After averaging double digits in both tackles for loss and QB hits from 2017 through 2023, Davis has averaged just 5.5 tackles for loss and two QB hits his last two seasons. In addition, after being above average in coverage most of his career, Davis is now a liability there, allowing a 110 passer rating last season. How much does Davis have left in the tank, and will he fall off a cliff this season? Who knows? As Billy Beane was told in Moneyball, “we’re all told at some point in time that we can no longer play the children’s game … some of us are told at eighteen, some of us are told at forty, but we’re all told.”

Jamien Sherwood had a breakout to the upside in 2024, but he fell back with a thud in 2025, wilting under the pressure of being THE GUY at linebacker. Now Sherwood has relinquished that role to Davis. Will he return to his prior form of 2024?

EDGE

The Jets had a very bad pass rushing group in 2025 with Will McDonald the only decent pass rusher. They tried to address that weakness by bringing in Joseph Ossai and Kingsley Enagbare in free agency, while also drafting David Bailey with the 2nd overall pick in the 2026 NFL draft. However, Enagbare has never had more than 4.5 sacks in a season. Ossai has never had more than five. Ossai is also sidelined with a foot injury that will require multiple weeks to heal and could hobble him most of the season. Bailey by all counts looked very good in training camp, but he’s a rookie who will likely take time developing into a force in the NFL. Can Enagbare improve his pass rush? Will Ossai be healthy and effective? Can Bailey thrive as a rookie? What can Will McDonald accomplish in a reduced role? Who knows? Nothing but question marks on the edge.

Interior defensive line

This appears to be a solid group. The main questions revolve around age related decline. Harrison Phillips turns 31 years old in January. David Onyemata turns 34 in November. Those are advanced years for NFL players, but neither player appears to be in serious decline thus far. Perhaps they need to take reduced snaps this year, but with young dudes like Jowon Briggs and T’Vondre Sweat more than capable starters, this group seems fairly deep and set up for success, barring multiple serious injuries.

SPECIAL TEAMS

The Jets seem in good shape at the returner positions with Isaiah Williams and Kene Nwangwu both well above average. Nwangwu, however, is always a question mark with his long injury history.

Austin McNamara is one of the best punters in the NFL. No questions there as long as he stays healthy.

At kicker the Jets had a close to automatic guy in Nick Folk last year. They chose to move on, probably because of his advanced age. That may prove to be a costly mistake. The Jets moved through a carousel of tryouts at kicker in the offseason. They ultimately claimed Blake Grupe on waivers and signed Jason Sanders to the practice squad. Neither option seems like a particularly safe bet. The Jets seem to concur, as they have continued to bring in kickers for tryouts even after bringing in Grupe. This position seems poised to implode on the Jets. Hopefully Grupe, or some undetermined other dude, proves me wrong.

item.title: Former Bears FB Matt Suhey dies at 68
item.description: Matt Suhey, a member of the Bears' Super Bowl XX champions, has died.
item.content:encoded:
Matt Suhey, a member of the Bears' Super Bowl XX champions, has died.

The Bears confirmed to the Associated Press that Suhey died at the age of 68. No cause of death was given.

Suhey was a 1980 second-round pick after playing at Penn State and spent most of his 10 seasons with the Bears as a lead blocker for Walter Payton. That run included the franchise's only Super Bowl win and Suhey ran for his only career postseason touchdown in Chicago's rout of the Patriots that secured the Lombardi Trophy.

Suhey, who spent his entire career with the Bears, ran 898 times for 2,946 yards and 20 touchdowns in 148 regular season games. He also caught 260 passes for 2,113 yards and five touchdowns over his decade in the NFL.

item.title: Notre Dame Football Stats: Week 1 Review of Win over Wisconsin
item.description: Let’s take a look at the numbers from Notre Dame’s 41-13 win over Wisconsin.
item.content:encoded:
Another Notre Dame college football season opener is in the books and there are two constants for me:

  • Dealing with the traditional, emotional first game roller coaster despite how much I convinced myself this time would be different
  • Stumbling through how to tell an analytics story without any real points of reference

Fortunately, the Irish delivered a big win that made all of the Week 1 stress worth it.  

Big Picture

The final score for the game was 41-13 and Notre Dame had a solid handle on things from beginning to end. Most of the not fun moments for ND fans were concentrated in the game’s first half. 

Notre Dame outscored Wisconsin 10-3 in the first quarter and the Badgers flipped the script with a 7-3 run to close out the second quarter.  But the Irish recorded 14 points in each of the remaining quarters while Wisconsin was only able to score three in the third quarter.

Yardage Summary

The Irish were +66 in total yards earned during their Week 1 matchup, tallying up 350 yards compared with the Badgers’ 284 yards. And they had the advantage in both the passing and rushing categories. 

Mike Denbrock’s offense was +22 in passing yards, edging out Wisconsin 239-217. The details behind both team’s passing performances were pretty similar. They both logged 19 pass completions, though Wisconsin made 30 attempts and Notre Dame made 29 attempts. One of the biggest passing blemishes for the game landed on the Wisconsin side, with one interception thrown late in the third quarter.

Notre Dame had a substantial rushing advantage. They beat out Wisconsin with a +44 differential, out earning their opponent 111-67 on the ground. But neither squad was particularly efficient in terms of rushing. The Irish had 32 rush attempts and finished with an average of 3.5 yards per attempt. The Badgers closed out things with 31 carries and averaged 2.2 yards per carry. 

The Quarterback Stats

C.J. Carr got the 2026-27 season started in a solid way, picking up where he left off from last year’s standout freshman performance. Carr threw the ball more in the season opener than he did on average last season but all the other stats held mostly the same.  He completed 19 of his attempts for a 66% completion rate. He logged 239 yards and also threw two passing touchdowns. 

The Rushers

Notre Dame continued the recent tradition of utilizing a rushing committee, with three running backs carrying the load in Week 1.

  • Junior running back Aneyas Williams led the group with 20 carries for 90 yards. He averaged 4.5 yards per carry and was responsible for both of the team’s collective rushing touchdowns. 

The Receivers

  • Senior Jordan Faison led the receiver room during Week 1 with four catches for 81 yards.
  • Sophomore running back Nolan James Jr. stood out as the Irish’s most prominent dual threat. James Jr. had seven rush attempts for 19 yards but produced significantly more in the receiving category.  He closed out the Wisconsin game with four catches for 67 yards and one touchdown through the air.
  • Junior wide receiver Micah Gilbert logged three receptions for 34 yards and senior tight end Cooper Flanagan pulled down two catches for 13 yards.

The Defensive Stats

Notre Dame’s defense got off to a slow start but turned things around.

Senior linebacker Kahanu Kia recovered a fumble on special teams and senior cornerback DJ McKinney was responsible for a 55-yard interception return for a touchdown. 

The Irish defensive unit finished Week 1 with two sacks, six tackles for loss and five pass deflections. 

  • Senior defensive lineman Boubacar Traore knabbed three solo tackles, one sack and two tackles for loss.
  • Junior defensive lineman Francis Brewu closed out the Wisconsin game with three tackles, one sack and one tackle for loss.
  • Sophomore cornerback Jayden Sanders led the secondary with two pass deflections.  
  • The remaining deflections were spread across cornerbacks DJ McKinney and Leonard more as well as safety Brauntae Johnson. 

The Flow Stats

One of the most reassuring things about how Notre Dame won their season opener was the offensive stability that emerged as the game progressed.

The team’s first scoring drive was capped off with a field goal and took four plays spanning 48 yards.  They scored a passing touchdown built on a four-play, 13-yard drive to close out the first quarter. But the rest of the Irish’s points resulted from long, relatively efficient drives:

Closing Thoughts

It was a solid start to the 2026-27 CFB season for Notre Dame. Would it have been great if my stress levels were just a smidge lower during the first half? A resounding yes.

But we’ve got a long fall of football ahead of us and this performance has me feeling pretty optimistic about what the Irish can deliver.
